clinician.trajectory_summary: 37-year-old Hispanic male from Honduras with remote history of Taenia solium (tapeworm) infection as a teenager presented to primary care with subacute episodic vertigo, nausea, left-sided tinnitus, and hearing loss exacerbated by dehydration and salty foods. Neurological examination was normal except for dizziness on Hallpike maneuver without nystagmus. Audiological evaluation revealed significant low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) in the left ear, with bilateral low-frequency SNHL developing within one year—findings initially consistent with Meniere's disease. However, MRI brain imaging revealed postinflammatory calcifications in the right parietal lobe (3 mm) and generalized volume loss more significant than expected for the patient's age. These imaging findings, in the context of the patient's remote tapeworm exposure and endemic origin, confirmed the diagnosis of neurocysticercosis rather than Meniere's disease. The postinflammatory nature of the calcification indicates chronic or resolved disease phase.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Although the clinical presentation (episodic vertigo, tinnitus, hearing loss, low-frequency SNHL) and audiological findings were initially consistent with Meniere's disease, the MRI brain findings of postinflammatory calcifications in the right parietal lobe and generalized volume loss more significant than expected for age are not explained by Meniere's disease and instead support neurocysticercosis. The patient's remote tapeworm exposure and endemic origin from Honduras further support neurocysticercosis as the underlying diagnosis.

remaining_uncertainties: Serological confirmation of cysticercosis (serum or CSF antibodies to Taenia solium) was not documented in available records
Complete inventory of all lesions on MRI beyond the right parietal calcification was not fully detailed

Anatomical explanation for how the right parietal lesion produces left-sided vestibular symptoms remains unclear; possible explanations include multiple lesions affecting vestibular pathways or the parietal lesion being incidental to the vestibular syndrome
Treatment initiated after neurocysticercosis diagnosis (anthelmintic agents, corticosteroids, anticonvulsants) was not documented
Clinical response to treatment and final clinical status/outcome were not documented
No documented seizures or loss of consciousness in the available history, though these would be expected manifestations of active neurocysticercosis

evaluation.known_final_diagnosis: The MRI revealed a 3 mm postinflammatory calcification in the right parietal lobe, thus confirming a diagnosis of neurocysticercosis (Fig. 3).
